exemplar: Garrison rejects gradualism entirely: he demands immediate abolition and vows to attack slavery with uncompromising, even harsh, moral force, refusing all moderation or retreat.

The expansion of slavery into new western territories - especially after the Missouri Compromise debates - convinced immediatists like Garrison that slavery was an aggressive power that had to be confronted, not accommodated.

The immediate-abolitionist movement Garrison launched helped polarize the nation: The Liberator's uncompromising moral attack on slavery as sin pushed the slavery controversy to the center of American politics in the 1830s and beyond.
parts: A. Briefly describe Garrison's position on how slavery should be opposed, as expressed in the excerpt.
B. Briefly explain ONE development of the 1820s that encouraged immediatist abolitionism.
C. Briefly explain ONE effect of Garrison's immediatist movement on American politics.

stimulus.attribution: William Lloyd Garrison, 'To the Public,' The Liberator, January 1, 1831.
stimulus.text: I will be as harsh as truth, and as uncompromising as justice. On this subject, I do not wish to think, or speak, or write, with moderation... I am in earnest - I will not equivocate - I will not excuse - I will not retreat a single inch - AND I WILL BE HEARD.

exemplar: The painting presents Columbus's landing as a triumphant, almost sacred moment of discovery - a heroic European arrival that frames the encounter from the European perspective.
The Columbian Exchange that followed brought devastating diseases such as smallpox to Native peoples, who had no immunity, killing vast numbers across the Caribbean within a generation.

Native peoples were not passive: they resisted conquest through rebellion, adapted European goods and animals to their own purposes, and maintained communities and cultures despite catastrophic losses.
parts: A. Briefly describe how the painting portrays Columbus's arrival in the Americas.
B. Briefly explain ONE consequence of the Columbian Exchange for Native peoples of the Caribbean.
C. Briefly explain ONE way Native peoples responded to European colonization.

stimulus.attribution: Described from John Vanderlyn's Landing of Columbus (1847), in the Rotunda of the U.S. Capitol.
stimulus.text: The painting shows Christopher Columbus and his men coming ashore, with Columbus planting the Spanish banner while kneeling in apparent reverence. Native inhabitants watch from the edges of the scene. The composition centers the Europeans as the agents of history, bathed in dramatic light.
